lines: Watch what happens before the bill, not after it. One missing filter, one full table scan, and nothing in the path stops it.
Now watch the same query with a cap configured. It fails in an instant, and nothing was ever charged at all.
Before I answer, separate two different jobs a control can do. One tells you something happened. The other refuses to let it happen.
Of these four, which one actually stops the money, rather than reporting on it afterward?
answer: A guardrail that refuses to run before the cost is incurred at all.
A tag and an alert both fire after the spend already happened. Only a check that runs before execution can keep the cost from existing.

lines: Notice where this check actually happens. Not after the query runs — before a single byte is read.
The engine estimates what the query would scan, compares that estimate to your limit, and only lets it through if it fits.
Resist the urge to treat auto-suspend and a resource monitor as the same kind of thing. One reacts to time. The other reacts to spend.
Together they close a gap a tag alone never could: an idle warehouse stops billing on its own, and a credit threshold can suspend it outright.
Watch what this tag actually changes, and what it doesn't. It shows up correctly later, in the billing record, attributed to the right budget.
What it never does is stop a single dollar from being spent — which makes it a completely different tool from a guardrail that blocks.
Here's the trade being made, in plain terms. A steep discount, in exchange for losing the instance on short notice, at any time.
Watch the checkpoint do its job: when the preemption actually hits, only the work since the last save gets redone, not the whole thing.
Don't treat this as a simple discount. It's a bet on how much you'll actually use, stretched across a multi-year term.
Below a certain utilization, paying full price the whole time would genuinely have cost less than the commitment did.
Notice this gate doesn't care whether the code is correct. It cares whether the bill for running it crossed a line.
Cross that line on this run, and the build goes red — exactly the way a failed test would, with nobody needing to notice the invoice days later.
If you only remember one line: some of these controls block, and some of them only label — and mixing the two up is the actual risk.
A cap and a monitor stop money from leaving. A tag just explains where it went. A discount trades flexibility for price. And now, even the bill itself can fail a build.
Before I answer, picture the job running overnight, unattended, with nobody watching a dashboard until morning.
Of everything covered tonight, which single change would have actually stopped the cost, not just reported it the next day?
answer: Configuring a byte cap that fails the query before it runs.
A tag only labels spend after it happens. Preemptible compute changes who can interrupt the job, not what it costs per byte. Only the cap itself runs before the charge.
